title: Ultra-tough, self-healing, n-type liquid crystal elastomer thermoelectric lonogels via synergistic hydrogen-bonds and electrostatic interaction

segments.text: Ionic thermoelectric (i-TE) materials have been regarded as promising candidates for the effective utilization of low-grade thermal energy due to their excellent thermopower and flexibility.

However, current research primarily focuses on p-type materials and thermopower optimization, with a lack of studies on n-type materials and the trade-off between thermoelectric performance and practical applicability.
Herein, we report an n-type liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) i-TE film that exhibits outstanding thermoelectric performance, ultra-stretchability, selfhealing, and freezing resistance.

Benefiting from multiple hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions between ions and LCE molecular chains, as well as phase separation effects, this film exhibits n-type characteristics while achieves a maximum tensile strain of 1570% and tensile strength of 2.85 MPa, and demonstrates self-healing within 3 h at room temperature.
Additionally, the LCE i-TE film shows great freezing resistance and durability, maintaining over 95% of its thermopower after liquid nitrogen immersion or 1000 stretching cycles, respectively.
Meanwhile, this LCE i-TE film can generate an open-circuit voltage of 6.3 mV under a small temperature difference of 1.8 K (human contact).

This multifunctional LCE i-TE film not only provides a new strategy for developing i-TE materials with n-type thermoelectric and superior mechanical properties, but also broadens the potential in flexible wearable, extreme, high-intensity scenarios.

title: Selective Regulation of Electron-Ion-Phonon Transport in Thermoelectric Materials toward High Performance and Stability

segments.text: The complex inter-relationships among electrons, ions, and phonons make it extremely challenging to simultaneously regulate these microscopic particles.
Superionic conductors offer an ideal operating platform but are often limited by their inherent ion mobility and susceptibility to degradation under extreme conditions.
We developed a strategy to improve the stability of ion-conducting thermoelectric materials by constructing an in situ ligand-derived organic-inorganic interface.
This strategy selectively enhances the electrical conductivity while suppressing the ionic and thermal conductivity.
The resulting materials are classified as phonon liquid electron crystal ionic insulators (PLECII).
The PLECII effectively prevents the accumulation of liquid-like ions under conditions of high current density and elevated temperature.
Additionally, this strategy decouples the transport of electrons, ions, and phonons, resulting in an exceptional thermoelectric performance.
Notably, a record-high energy conversion efficiency of 4.0% was achieved in the Cu2S-based device at a temperature difference of 473.1 K.
Our method enables the design of materials with tunable electrical, ionic, and thermal conductivity, thereby expanding the applications of superionic conductors.
